title: In-cell structures visualize human pre-ribosome assembly in the nucleolus.
data_url: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb/EMD-59086 (23 EMDB maps, EMD-58993/59048/59068-59088); EMPIAR-13880 (raw, not yet released); https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22237116

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded EMD-59086 (46 MB gzipped) from the EMDB FTP site and parsed its MRC header and voxel array myself: 234x234x234 voxels, 3.425 Angstrom per voxel, 801.45 Angstrom box, float32 densities (min -0.0055, max 0.0213). Queried the EMDB application programming interface for all 23 maps from this paper and read out their state names, resolutions (6.9-19.4 Angstrom) and subtomogram counts (e.g. pre-60S consensus 183,293 particles from 305 tomograms; SSU processome consensus 51,498). Listed the EMDB folders: only maps, half-maps, masks and Fourier shell correlation curves are deposited, no particle tables. Read the Zenodo record metadata: two PyMOL session files totalling 5.88 GB, CC-BY-4.0, and confirmed the 1.80 GB file serves HTTP 200. Confirmed EMPIAR-13880 is NOT downloadable: its FTP directory returns 404 while a control entry (EMPIAR-11472) returns 200. The BioImage Archive accession quoted in the data statement (S-BIAP4028) returns 0 hits in BioStudies.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The data availability wording (EMPIAR-13880, BioImage Archive, Zenodo, 'accessions in Table S1') came from a web summary of the Science paper and the bioRxiv preprint, not from a full text I retrieved: Science is paywalled, there is no PubMed Central identifier, and bioRxiv rate-limited every attempt to fetch the full text or its XML. So the per-state particle numbers I report are EMDB's own metadata, not numbers I read in the paper.

a1_downloadable.note: The 23 EMDB density maps download freely and open (I parsed one). But the only deposit that could ever carry per-particle labels, EMPIAR-13880, is not released: its FTP folder 404s while a control EMPIAR entry returns 200. The quoted BioImage Archive accession also does not resolve.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. There is no label column anywhere. The only structured outputs are 23 averaged three-dimensional density maps, each carrying a state name in its title. Any per-particle label (which assembly state a given molecule is in) would have to be constructed by re-running three-dimensional classification on raw tomograms that are not public.

a3_inputs_present.note: The inputs that do exist are present as real volumes, not accession pointers: I read the voxel data of EMD-59086 directly. But they are 23 class averages, not per-example inputs.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are explicit and consistent: voxel spacing 3.425 Angstrom, box 801.45 Angstrom, resolution in Angstrom by Fourier shell correlation at the 0.143 cut-off, recorded in the EMDB metadata I read.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. 23 labelled items (23 EMDB maps across roughly 6 SSU processome states and 16 pre-60S states), far under the ~400 floor for classification. The 183,293 pre-60S and 51,498 SSU processome subtomograms exist only inside the unreleased EMPIAR deposit.

a6_fits_laptop.note: All 23 maps are about 2.2 GB gzipped and a single map is 51 MB in memory as float32, so the released slice fits a 16 GB laptop. The particle-level route would need multi-terabyte tomograms and a graphics processing unit, so it does not.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: EMDB metadata is internally consistent (305 tomograms, 1,284,773 extracted pre-60S picks, 183,293 in the consensus average). I could not cross-check against the paper: Science is paywalled, there is no PubMed Central copy, and bioRxiv rate-limited every full-text request.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL for the only project worth doing here. The 'assembly state' of each particle is the output of the authors' own three-dimensional classification run in Warp/RELION, i.e. an algorithm's assignment to a cluster, not an independent physical measurement. Training a model to predict it distils their classification pipeline, and its ceiling is that pipeline's accuracy.

existing_models.name: TomoTwin (Nature Methods 2023), a deep metric-learning particle picker for cryo-electron tomograms
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported as a general picking model usable without retraining per protein; benchmarked on its own tomogram sets, no split comparable to anything available here.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Picking small, low-contrast and crowded complexes inside cells remains hard.

existing_models.name: DeePiCt (deep picker in context, Nature Methods 2022), supervised segmentation and complex localisation in cryo-electron tomography
existing_models.score_and_split: Evaluated on annotated Schizosaccharomyces pombe tomograms; used to separate compositionally distinct ribosome subpopulations.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Low-abundance, low-density complexes and the shortage of expert-annotated training tomograms.

existing_models.name: tomoDRGN (Nature Methods 2024), a neural network that learns structural heterogeneity from cryo-electron subtomograms
existing_models.score_and_split: Demonstrated on in-situ subtomogram sets; recovers continuous and discrete conformational variation.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Interpreting learned latent spaces and linking them to discrete biological states.

existing_models.name: DISCA (PNAS 2023), unsupervised deep iterative subtomogram clustering
existing_models.score_and_split: Clusters subtomograms into structural patterns without labels; evaluated on simulated and real tomograms.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Validating that discovered clusters correspond to real distinct complexes.

backbone.name: None that fits. Three-dimensional convolutional networks or tomoDRGN-style encoders would be the right family, but 23 class-average volumes is not a training set for any of them.
backbone.hardware: Graphics processing unit required for any real subtomogram work; the released maps need none because there is nothing to train on.
backbone.licence: EMDB maps are public domain (CC0-equivalent); the Zenodo PyMOL sessions are CC-BY-4.0.

integration.partner_dataset: Ex-situ (purified-sample) pre-ribosome structures in EMDB and the Protein Data Bank from the Klinge and Hurt laboratories, plus the Chlamydomonas in-situ nucleolar tomography dataset (Nature Communications 2021).
integration.join_key: Assembly-state name matched by hand (state A, B, C...), plus EMDB accession; there is no machine-readable shared identifier.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a pre-ribosome pass through the same ordered sequence of states inside a living nucleolus as it does in a test tube, and does its position in the nucleolus tell you which state it is in? Real question, but answering it needs the per-particle coordinates and state calls that are locked inside the unreleased EMPIAR-13880 deposit.

controls.positive_control: A model would have to re-find the known ex-situ pre-60S state order; nothing to run it on, so this is hypothetical.
controls.negative_control: Not runnable: no per-example table to shuffle.
controls.external_validation: The Chlamydomonas in-situ nucleolar tomography study (Nature Communications 2021) measured the same kind of maturation gradient in a different organism, so it would be a genuine external check if the particle tables ever become public.

honest_claim_h3: With the data that is actually public, the only honest claim is a description of 23 averaged density maps at 6.9-19.4 Angstrom; no model trained on them could claim anything about individual molecules, because every per-molecule measurement sits in an unreleased archive.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a pre-ribosome's position inside the nucleolus to predict which assembly stage it has reached.
plain_idea.train_on: Ideally one row per imaged molecule: its three-dimensional position in the tomogram, its distance to the nucleolar sub-compartment boundaries, which cell it came from, and whether the cell was treated with an RNA polymerase I inhibitor. The authors have about 183,293 pre-60S and 51,498 SSU processome particles, but that per-particle table is not public; only 23 group averages are.
plain_idea.predict: Which of roughly 22 assembly states the particle belongs to. The 'true answer' is the cluster the authors' three-dimensional classification software assigned it to, which is an algorithm's call on a noisy density volume, not a separate measurement.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Ribosome-assembly and nucleolus biologists want to know whether the nucleolus is a spatial assembly line, so that position predicts maturity; a clear answer would change how people interpret every nucleolar image. As things stand the inputs for that question are not downloadable.

more_or_better_data.why: We have 23 averaged maps. TomoTwin, DeePiCt, tomoDRGN and DISCA were each developed on whole annotated tomogram sets with per-particle ground truth; the comparable data here (305 tomograms, 1.28 million extracted picks) is in EMPIAR-13880, which is not released.

confidence_score.why: No per-example data, so no way to estimate per-prediction uncertainty. The half-maps give a map-level resolution estimate only, which is not a prediction confidence.

models_beatable.why: The relevant tools are 2022-2024, open-source, with published evaluations on annotated tomograms; without the raw tomograms we cannot even run one as a baseline, let alone beat it.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition: no existing model can be run as a baseline here, because the input data those models consume (tomograms and particle coordinates) is not downloadable.

ml_idea: The idea considered and rejected: train a classifier that predicts a pre-ribosome's assembly state from its position inside the nucleolus (distance to the dense fibrillar component and granular component boundaries), tested by holding out whole cells, with the RNA polymerase I inhibition condition as a perturbation test. It dies because the per-particle coordinate-and-state table that this needs has not been released, and because the state labels are a classification algorithm's output rather than an independent measurement.

effort.compute_note: Measured directly: one map is 46 MB gzipped and 51 MB as a float32 array in memory, so all 23 maps are about 2.2 GB on disk and comfortably under 16 GB of RAM. No cross-validation time is estimable because there is no trainable table; any particle-level version would need multi-terabyte tomograms and a graphics processing unit.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: One HTTP request to the EMPIAR-13880 FTP directory. It returns 404 while a control entry returns 200, which kills the project in under a minute.

verdict_reason: Fails A2, A5 and A8. The public data is 23 averaged three-dimensional density maps (verified by downloading and parsing one), which is a structural-biology result, not a training set: there is no label column, 23 items is far under the ~400 floor, and the state labels are the authors' own three-dimensional classification output rather than an independent measurement. The per-particle table that would make this interesting (183,293 pre-60S and 51,498 SSU processome subtomograms with positions and state calls) sits in EMPIAR-13880, whose FTP directory returns 404 while a control entry returns 200, so it is not released. Worth re-checking in six to twelve months: if EMPIAR-13880 goes live with particle coordinates and class assignments, the spatial-gradient question becomes a genuine, laptop-scale tabular project.
